paper_title: Periodic Weak Spots: Phase Sensitivity from Chunked KV-Cache Compression

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Chunked KV-cache compression reduces the memory and attention costs of long-context inference by compressing windows of consecutive tokens into fewer cache entries at a fixed stride. Such compression also introduces a new positional coordinate: a token's phase, or its position relative to compression-window boundaries. We uncover a systematic asymmetry in models using such compression: the same information can be easy to retrieve at one phase and difficult at another. We call this periodic variation in retrieval performance phase sensitivity. In large open-weight models with such compression, long-context retrieval accuracy can differ by up to 40 percentage points across phases, revealing periodic weak spots that average benchmark scores can conceal. To investigate this behavior, we pretrain a family of transformers from scratch across multiple KV-compression designs, reproducing phase sensitivity across the variants. Mechanistic analysis using causal interventions in these models reveals phase specialization: different attention components contribute asymmetrically to retrieving information at different source phases. We further analyze idealized retrieval models, showing how gradient flow dynamics may favor sharp phase specialization. Evaluating models with chunked KV-cache compression thus requires measuring across compression phases: high average accuracy can coexist with systematic positional failures.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Long-context inference in transformers can be bottlenecked by the KV cache, whose memory and attention costs grow with context length. practical remedy, used in models such as DeepSeek-V4 [11], is chunked KV-cache compression: the model groups consecutive tokens into fixed-size windows, compresses each window into fewer cache entries, and uses these summaries for long-context retrieval [28, 36]. The compression happens as context is processed, before later query specifies what information will need to be recalled. Each summary is therefore query-agnostic and must preserve information that may be needed later. 1 This design imposes periodic structure on the context. new compression window begins every tokens, where is the compression stride. Each token thus has new coordinate relative to these boundaries beyond its absolute position. We call this coordinate its phase, defined as its position modulo S. Shifting the input by few tokens can change which tokens are compressed together without changing their content or relative positions. The same information may thus be compressed differently depending on its phase, and hence retained with different fidelity. In LLMs trained with chunked KV-cache compression, we find that retrieval performance varies sharply and periodically with the phase of the source information, failure mode we term phase sensitivity (Section 2). motivating example comes from asking DeepSeek-V4 to complete its own inference code (Figure 1). When we prepend decorative comment and vary only its length, the models preferred completion of one token flips with period of four tokens, matching its compression stride. We then measure retrieval directly through controlled needle-in-a-haystack evaluation (Figure 2). At 128K context, retrieval accuracy in the DeepSeek-V4 family can differ by up to 40 percentage points across phases. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report of such internal periodic variation, which average benchmark scores can conceal. To test whether chunked KV compression is the source of such variation, we pretrain from scratch broad family of transformers with the Qwen3-0.6B architecture [27] as backbone and KV compression as the only substantial architectural modification (Section 3). Every compressed model we evaluate shows periodicity matching the compression stride, including models that simply average token representations within each window. By contrast, full-attention baselines have no comparable periodicity. natural first explanation is the window boundary itself. In our needle-in-a-haystack task, each key is immediately followed by its value, so with non-overlapping windows keyvalue pair either falls inside one window or is split across two, and split pair is plausibly harder to retrieve. However, boundaries alone do not account for the full periodic pattern: accuracy also varies widely across phases that keep the key and its value within single window. This suggests deeper look into how the model writes information into compressed memory and reads it back. Causal interventions on KV heads and layers support this view: retrieval at different phases depends differently on different heads, systematic pattern we call phase specialization (Section 4.1). The pattern appears in both our pretrained models and DeepSeek-V4. To examine how such specialization can develop, we study compression gates, which determine how much each within-window position contributes to compressed entry (Section 4.2). In pretrained model whose gates can learn separate positional preferences, some heads develop persistent preferences during pretraining that recur across inputs. Their intervention effects are strongest near the phases they favor, supporting division of retrieval work among the examined heads. The emergence of these preferences suggests that training can favor selective retention even when future queries are unknown. We examine this possibility in an idealized induction task with compressed attention (Section 5), where mixing information in the compression window can weaken the match between compressed key and later query. We show that the optimal compressor favors particular phases, and gradient flow drives gates toward persistent preferences. Together, these findings show that average accuracy is not enough to evaluate models with chunked KV-cache compression. Their reliability should also be measured across phases, for example by shifting the input by few tokens while keeping the queried information fixed.

sections.title: 2.1 A Periodically Flipping Code-Completion Example
sections.content: We begin by asking DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base to complete DeepSeek-V4s official inference code (Figure 1a). The prompt ends at FP inside type cast in an FP8 quantization function, and the original source continues with 8. The surrounding code favors this continuation. The function quantizes to FP8, while the outer cast already converts to compute_dtype, which is FP32. Completing 32 would duplicate the outer cast and skip the rounding step. To test whether this prediction depends on position, we prepend decorative docstring and vary its length by changing the number of repeated = characters on its second line. The code is unchanged, and each additional filler token shifts the code and the completion position by one. Across 16 filler lengths from 2 Figure 1 Next-token predictions by DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base on code snippet. The prediction flip periodically as variable-length decorative filler shifts the input. (a) The decorative filler is docstring whose length varies by the number of = characters. The ground-truth completion is 8, supported by the highlighted components in the context. (b) Averaged over the eight lengths in each group, the model places higher probability on the incorrect 32 when mod 4 {0, 1} and on the correct 8 when mod 4 {2, 3}. (c) The preferred completion switches every two tokens and the pattern repeats every four, matching DeepSeek-V4s compression stride. 24 to 39 tokens, the top-1 prediction flips periodically (Figure 1b,c). In particular, the model predicts 8 when mod 4 {2, 3} and 32 at the remaining eight lengths, and (8) (32) ranges from 0.79 to 0.95. Changing only the docstring length thus reverses the preferred continuation. The reversals repeat every four tokens, matching the stride = 4 of DeepSeek-V4s compressed sparse attention (CSA). This match suggests that the prediction depends on where the code falls relative to the compression windows. The reversals are not limited to one filler. In all four filler families we tested, most predictions follow the same four-token pattern (Appendix B.1), and the post-trained DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 and DeepSeek-V4.1Flash [12] also show periodic reversals under several filler sweeps, matching their compression strides (S = 4 and = 2 respectively). In contrast, DeepSeek-V3.1-Base, without chunked KV compression, ranks 32 above 8 at only 4 of the same 64 inputs, with very small margins (Appendix B.2). We give the exact inputs, results for the other models, and two further code-completion examples in Appendix B.

sections.title: 2.2 Measuring Phase Sensitivity in Retrieval
sections.content: To measure this effect more systematically, we turn to controlled keyvalue based retrieval task in which we can measure the models capability of retrieving the same piece of information, but at different relative positions with respect to the compression boundaries. For compression stride S, we call mod the phase of key-value pair starting at position t, and we say that retrieval is phase-sensitive when certain retrieval metric, such as accuracy or the probability assigned to the correct answer, changes systematically with the phase of the source. We evaluate the base and post-trained versions of DeepSeek-V4-Flash and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, as well as the post-trained DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, on single-token needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH) retrieval. Each 128K-token prompt holds 16k keyvalue pairs and asks for the value of source key near its middle (Figure 2a). We sort the prompts into eight residue groups by the source keys position modulo eight, which covers two stride cycles for DeepSeek-V4 and four for DeepSeek-V4.1. All groups share the same prompt length, query position, and keyvalue bindings, and we choose their filler lengths so that the mean and variance of the source keys absolute position are the same in every group. We defer details about the construction of the retrieval dataset to Appendix C.1. In Figure 2, we can see that the base checkpoints are sharply phase-sensitive, with maximum gaps of up to 40.2 percentage points. Post-training raises accuracy and narrows these gaps, but the gaps of the post-trained DeepSeek-V4 models remain large. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash has the smallest gap, yet all four of its even residue 3 Figure 2 NIAH retrieval accuracy of DeepSeek-V4 family for key-value pairs with different offsets. All five models exhibit phase sensitivity, with period of 2 or 4 matching the CSA stride. An answer counts as correct if, after stripping whitespace, it begins with the gold value. The marker for residue of the target keys position modulo 8 sits between ticks and r+1. Gray bands mark stride boundaries, shading shows two-sided 95% Wilson intervals, and is the best-to-worst gap. groups remain above all four odd ones. Average accuracy alone can conceal these differences across phases.

sections.title: 3 Controlled Pretraining Studies
sections.content: DeepSeek-V4 differs from standard transformer in many ways besides chunked KV compression, and we cannot retrain it without compression to see whether the periodicity disappears. To test whether chunked compression is the source of phase sensitivity, we pretrain Qwen3-derived family of models from scratch in which chunked compression is the only substantial architectural change, together with full-attention baselines trained the same way. We also vary how compression is performed to see which aspects of phase sensitivity, such as its period, depend on that design. These models also support the mechanistic analyses in Section 4.

sections.title: 3.2 Phase Sensitivity across the Kernel Family
sections.content: If phase sensitivity arises from chunked compression, compressed models should show it and full-attention baselines should not. We see this contrast in Figure 3. Every compressed model varies periodically with the source-key phase, including the DeepSeek-style kernel (Figure 3i), while the full-attention baselines stay flat (Figure 3a). The same holds for every compressed run in Table 8, with Prefix Padding gaps of up to 78 percentage points against at most 6.1 for the baselines. Note that summary metrics conceal much of this difference. With eight KV heads, the W8/S8 compressed model nearly matches its full-attention baseline in mean accuracy and validation loss, yet its worst residue is only 9.9%, against 58.4% for the baseline. At one and four KV heads, the compressed models reach higher mean accuracy than the baselines at comparable validation loss. Varying window and stride separately shows that the period follows the stride in the tested geometries, whether or not windows overlap. At = 8, strides {4, 6, 8} give periods of about four, six, and eight tokens (Figure 3bd). W4/S4 shares W8/S4s four-token period despite its smaller window (Figure 10), and W12/S12 produces an approximately twelve-token period (Figure 3e). In these experiments, phase sensitivity needs neither rotary position embeddings (RoPE) nor learned gates: it persists without RoPE (Figure 3h) and when uniform averaging replaces the gates (Figure 11). sections.title: 4 Phase Specialization
sections.content: Retrieval at each phase runs through the attention heads that write and read compressed entries, and head may serve some phases more reliably than others. We call this phase specialization: the contributions of some heads to retrieval depend systematically on phase, so different heads contribute asymmetrically to information at different phases. The definition presupposes no cause, whether boundary straddling or within-window differences. We measure this asymmetry with knockouts in our pretrained models and DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base (Section 4.1), and then examine sharper form in one model, where heads preference for some phases is also visible in how it compresses (Section 4.2).

sections.content: To find which heads matter for retrieval at each phase, we knock out one KV head at time [24, 38] and see where accuracy drops. The model without chunked KV compression (a) shows uniform horizontal stripes across residue groups, indicating that each layer contributes similarly at every source position, while the models with chunked KV compression (b,c) show heterogeneous patterns across the residues of the target key. In (c), the pattern also repeats with period four, matching the CSA stride, and the odd layers, which use heavily compressed attention (HCA) with compression rate 128, contribute little to retrieval. 6 calibration prompts. We adopt similar knockout strategy for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base and replace whole layers attention output at band of query suffix, with 256 evaluation prompts per residue group (see Appendix E.6 for details). We visualize the effect of knocking out each head on retrieval performance for information at each phase in Figure 4. The knockout maps differ between full attention and compression. In the full-attention baseline, the layers with large losses reduce accuracy by similar amounts at every position (Figure 4a). In the W8/S8 compressed model, some heads have losses concentrated on few phases, and different heads have different phase-dependent effects (Figure 4b). In DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base, the largest losses affect every phase unevenly and few earlier layers affect only some phases, repeating every four positions, its compression stride (Figure 4c). This pattern is not specific to one model. In Appendix F, we give knockout maps for every compressed model in Table 8 under both padding protocols. In most compressed models, some heads have losses concentrated on few phases that repeat every stride, and in the others, losses spread over all phases with periodic variation. With several KV heads, some individual heads still show losses concentrated on one or two phases, so the asymmetry is not only property of layers (Figure 9).

If learned gate preferences help determine which phases are retrieved well, cycling the offset-specific gate parameters by offsets should also approximately shift the accuracy pattern by phases. In Appendix H, we test this prediction in five models with gates exhibiting sharp static concentration (including the W8/S8 reference model). These interventions support causal contribution of learned gate preferences to within-window retrieval asymmetry in these models. We conjecture that the observed phase sensitivity in accuracy reflects both boundary and within-window asymmetries. The first distinguishes keyvalue pairs that share window from pairs that straddle one. The second concerns differences among phases within window, with static gate concentration as one mechanism that can shape which phases each head retains. Accuracy in the reference model varies by more than 50 percentage points among phases whose keyvalue pairs all share window (Section 3.2), while uniform averaging also exhibits within-window variation, showing that this second asymmetry can arise without learned gates.

sections.title: 5 Theory: Emergence of Phase Specialization in Compression
sections.content: In Section 4.2, some gates develop persistent preferences for the same offsets across windows, and these heads matter most at the corresponding phases. In an idealized induction model, we ask why compression should concentrate when the future query is unknown, why the concentration becomes static, and whether heads divide the phases among themselves.

sections.title: 6 Related Works
sections.content: Learned compressed memories reduce the cost of retaining long contexts. Compressive Transformer summarizes past activations [28], LoMA trains models to use compressed KV representations [36], Activation Beacon replaces raw activations with the KV entries of regularly spaced learned tokens [44], and CAT lets later chunks attend to compressed vectors of earlier chunks [25]. Sparse attention [8, 11, 20, 41] and cache eviction [18, 45] impose related block or token structure on memory. Sparse Transformer already defines strided head whose visibility depends on position modulo stride [8], precedent for the periodic structure we study. In hybrids that keep an exact branch over distant tokens, such as NSA [41], that branch could mask failure of the compressed branch alone. DeepSeek-V4 keeps exact tokens only in its local window [11], and we find phase sensitivity in the full models (Section 2). On the failure mode side, the Lost in the Middle effect shows that retrieval quality depends on where relevant information appears in long context [19]. RULER shows that easy needle tests can overstate usable context length [16], and Chen et al. [5] show that aggregate scores can hide method-specific failures of KV cache compression. In gist-based compression, Deng et al. [13] identify degradation near generation-segment boundaries. We instead focus on the phase of the source token, which recurs every compression stride and is distinct from overall context depth or the querys position within segment. Mechanistic studies identify retrieval heads whose ablation impairs long-context retrieval [38], and cache policies such as RazorAttention and DuoAttention keep full caches only for such heads [31, 39]. These works establish that heads differ in their retrieval roles. We show that in compressed models, heads retrieval contribution also depends on phase and, in the examined heads, aligns with the offsets its compression gate prefers (Section 4). On the theory side, gradient descent can turn softmax attention into hard token selectors [32, 33], and multi-head training dynamics can allocate tasks across heads [6, 42]. We do not claim the first theory of attention hardening or head specialization. Our analysis instead concerns compression chosen before the query is known, and asks when concentrated compression is optimal and when training makes it static (Section 5). We give more extensive discussion of related work in Appendix I.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion and Discussion
sections.content: In this paper, we identify phase sensitivity as systematic failure mode in models with chunk-compressed KV caches: retrieval accuracy depends on the source informations phase relative to the compression windows. The phenomenon appears in DeepSeek-V4, V4.1, and all compressed models we pretrained, with period following the compression stride. KV-head knockouts in our pretrained models and attention-readout interventions reveal phase-dependent contributions to retrieval, providing causal evidence for phase specialization in these tested models. Finally, our optimization dynamics analysis shows how training can produce static concentration of compression gates in simplified bigram retrieval model, illustrating mechanism for phase specialization under the stated assumptions. Our mechanistic conclusions are strongest in the controlled settings studied here and do not establish universal cause of phase sensitivity in large, heterogeneous models. In particular, gate cycling does not restore the boundary phase (Appendix H), leaving unified explanation of boundary and within-window asymmetries unresolved. Whether explicit coordination across heads and layers can make retrieval quality more uniform across phases, without sacrificing average performance or compression efficiency, remains open. Beyond controlled retrieval, our code-completion examples document periodic errors in DeepSeek-V4 and DeepSeek-V4.1. These observations motivate investigating whether phase sensitivity also affects robustnessrelevant behavior. For example, do meaning-preserving shifts of request within its context alter refusal or compliance, and do any such changes track the compression phase? We leave systematic study of their potential robustness implications in real application scenarios to future work.

A.1.2 From the Toy Example to the General Model The toy example isolates two pressures, one favoring sharp heads and one favoring balanced coverage of the phases. Sharpening comes from competition with the 1 distractor chunks. Because > 1, uniform head gives the correct chunk less than half of its attention, and in this regime the correct-chunk attention mass rises more when the target logit increases than it falls when the logit decreases by the same amount. head that moves toward one phase therefore gains more attention mass on that phase than it loses on the other, which raises the mean attention mass over the two phases (Equation (14)). Balance comes from the loss. Both heads add evidence to the same margin for each phase, and the logistic loss flattens as margin grows, so evidence added to the phase with the larger margin lowers the loss less than evidence added to the 19 phase with the smaller one. For fixed mean, the loss is therefore smallest when both phases receive the same attention mass. Both pressures are satisfied together only at the complementary endpoints, which is why these are the only global minimizers (Lemma 4). The same two pressures govern the dynamics. At the uniform point, the two heads are identical. Along the complementary direction (1, 1)/ 2, in which the heads move toward different phases, the two phases stay balanced, so only sharpening acts and trajectories escape at rate λesc. Along the common direction (1, 1)/ 2, in which both heads move toward the same phase, sharpening and balance compete. Condition (16) is sufficient for balance to win, which makes this direction stable and the uniform point saddle (Lemma 5). small random initialization therefore leaves the uniform point along the complementary direction and then stays near the complementary line. Both pressures reappear in the general model, but they change in different ways. Sharpening survives, but it now comes from pairing keys with values rather than from the asymmetry that > 1 provides. Under exact geometry, heads contribution to the target logit for query at position is its correct-chunk attention, which grows with its key weight at r, times its value weight at + 1. Because the value weights sum to one, this contribution summed over query positions is at most the attention that one-hot key receives, and it reaches that value only when the key coefficient is one-hot at some and the value coefficient is one-hot at + 1. In Appendix A.3, we use this bound to rule out mixed coefficients, in the role that Lemma 4 plays for the toy example. Balance, by contrast, becomes weak when the vocabulary is large. In that regime, the cross-entropy loss is nearly linear in the target logit, because its normalizer is dominated by the many vocabulary items that do not appear in the context. Under exact geometry, two heads that select the same position keep the same expected target logit and pay only through the normalizer, by an amount at most of order 1/N . This penalty still makes complementary coverage optimal when ε = 0 (Appendix A.3). Our dynamics proof, however, treats all normalizer terms as small perturbations, and the remaining target terms do not couple different heads, so the proof has no force that separates them (Appendix A.4). Unlike the toy example, Theorem 12 therefore guarantees persistent selection without guaranteeing complementary coverage. sections.content: Here we describe the architecture, attention memory, positional encoding, and training settings behind our pretrained models in Section 3. We report the complete sweep in Appendix F. D.1 Backbone and Compression Kernels Backbone and reference compression kernel. The Qwen3-0.6B backbone has 28 layers, hidden width 1,024, 16 query heads, and head dimension dh = 128. We retain its feed-forward blocks, residual connections, and normalization, so that chunked KV compression is the only substantial architectural change. The reference compression kernel uses non-overlapping windows with = = 8 and one KV head per layer (a keyvalue head, as opposed to the 16 query heads). Its K/V branches are separate and use scalar gates: payload maps are shared across offsets (C = B), while gate maps and biases depend on the offset. The same configuration is used in every layer. The ablations vary KV-head count, pooling, parameter sharing, gate dimensionality, positional bias, window overlap, positional encoding, normalization, and local-memory policy. Gate granularity and parameter sharing. Using the notation of Section 3.1, scalar gates have dg = 1, with one gate score per token broadcast across all projected dimensions. Vector gates have dg = dh, allowing projected dimensions to prefer different window offsets. Separate K/V branches use their own payload maps, gate maps, and positional biases. Tied K/V branches share all three and produce common compressed representation (cid:98)Kj = (cid:98)Vj, before the normalization and positional transformations described below. Within each branch, payload and gate maps can be shared independently across the whole window, within groups of offsets, or remain offset-specific. Sharing these maps does not require sharing positional biases across offsets. Uniform averaging fixes each gate-score coordinate at 1/W in full window. The evaluated configurations are listed in Table 8. DeepSeek-style compression kernel. Combining these options recovers DeepSeek-V4s CSA compression kernel [11], which lets us test whether the kernel studied in Section 2 produces phase sensitivity in our backbone. It uses = 8, = 4, vector gates, and tied K/V branches. The preceding four-token half, with offsets {0, 1, 2, 3}, uses the payload and gate maps (C(0), Z(0)). The current four-token half, with offsets {4, 5, 6, 7}, uses separate pair (C(1), Z(1)). Each pair is shared within its half. Positional biases remain offset-specific and are shared between the tied K/V branches. In full window, one softmax spans all eight offsets for each gate dimension. D.2 Windows, Attention Memory, and Positional Encoding Each kernel above produces one compressed entry per window. To use these entries in attention, we specify when each entry is emitted, which entries query sees alongside its local window, and at which position each entry is rotated. 43 Window indexing and initial boundary. Token positions start at zero, and compressed entries use one-based indices 1. Entry closes at jS 1 and pools offsets 0 < at source positions jS + i. Conversely, small knockout effect does not establish that component is unused: other components can compensate. sections.content: In Section 4.2, we found few gates with sharp offset preferences that persist across windows and inputs, and knocking out three of the corresponding heads in the reference model costs the most accuracy near the phases their gates favor. If such preferences help decide which phases are weak, editing them after training may move the weak phases with them. We test this by cycling each gates preference by fixed number of offsets and checking whether the accuracy pattern across phases shifts by as many phases. H.1 Gate Cycling In models with non-overlapping windows (W = S), window offset is also phase i. gates preference for offset comes from its gate map ZB (Section 3.1). Cycling by δ moves both forward by δ offsets, while the payload maps stay fixed: and positional gate bias bB (cid:101)ZB = ZB (iδ) mod , = bB (cid:101)bB (iδ) mod , {K, }. (118) The gate parameters of offset are thus applied at offset (i + δ) mod . We move maps and biases together, not the biases alone, because both enter the gate logits. The hidden states stay at their original offsets, so this does not move the realized gate scores exactly, and whether the preferences move with the parameters is an empirical question. In each experiment, we cycle the key and value gates of every head in layers 3 to 23 (zero-based) at step 47,518 and measure full-vocabulary top-1 accuracy on 1,000 logical examples of the retrieval task in Appendix C.2 with Prefix Padding, folding the 24 source-key residues modulo S. Away from the boundary phase, both cycles shift the accuracy pattern approximately as predicted (Figure 19), with R2 of 0.984 for δ = +1 and 0.995 for δ = 1 over comparisons in which phase 11 is neither the observed nor the source phase. sections.title: I Extended Related Work
sections.content: Learned summary memories. Compressive Transformer down-samples old activations into FIFO compressed memory using stride-matched pooling or convolution [28]. Gist tokens and Landmark Attention use special tokens to condense prompts or route random access to blocks [21, 22]. LoMA adds an explicit reconstruction objective [36]. Activation Beacon inserts regularly spaced learned beacon tokens whose KVs replace raw activations, and MELODI builds recurrent short-term memory across multiple layers and long-term memory in single middle layer [7, 44]. CAT is particularly close at the architectural level: later chunks attend to compressed prior-chunk vectors, and its appendix reports high loss at the first token of each new chunk and recall degradation as chunks grow [25]. None of these works examines retrieval as function of source phase within compressed memory. Cross-chunk failure modes. Deng et al. [13] systematically compare recurrent, coarse-KV, and fine-grained-KV gist compression. Their reconstruction probe shows severe information bottleneck as compression rises, and their lost by the boundary diagnostic finds segment-scale sawtooth: with 2K segments, generation is weakest immediately after segment boundary, when predictions depend most strongly on compressed prior segments, and improves as raw tokens accumulate in the current segment. They also document semantically surprising facts being dropped and long exact strings being lost during generation. KSAs chunk-aligned sliding window addresses separate case in which partially visible chunk is neither locally complete nor yet represented by summary [9]. HMT uses the phrase periodical recall pattern for successful tracking of an artificially periodic topic-switch sequence, not an architecture-induced failure [15]. Among these works, the sawtooth of Deng et al. [13] is the direct precedent for recurring cross-chunk degradation, but its phase variable is the query/generation position within the current 2K segment. Our phase variable is the source position modulo the much smaller compression stride inside already-compressed memory. Sparse and hybrid routing. Sparse Transformer explicitly defines strided head with modulo connectivity and notes that the pattern may route poorly on nonperiodic text [8]. It is thus precedent for residue-class visibility as general attention concept. NSA forms overlapping compressed block representations for coarse selection and retains an exact fine-grained branch [41]. MoBA routes queries to selected raw-token blocks [20], and the Sparse Frontier compares the qualityefficiency trade space across such sparse patterns [23]. DeepSeek-V4 selects sparsely among compressed KV entries and adds an uncompressed local window [11]. In hybrids with an exact branch over distant tokens, such as NSA, that branch could mask failure of the compressed branch alone. DeepSeek-V4 keeps exact tokens only in its local window, and in Section 2, we find phase sensitivity in the full models. Cache allocation and specialized retrieval components. H2O and SnapKV evict or cluster tokens using estimated importance [18, 45]. SqueezeAttention allocates different cache budgets across layers [37], while RazorAttention and DuoAttention retain long-range caches for retrieval heads and use compressed or streaming policies elsewhere [31, 39]. Wu et al. [38] causally identify small subset of heads that dominate long-context factual retrieval. Generic heterogeneity across heads and layers is therefore already established. Our empirical claim is more specific: KV-head knockouts in compressed models have phase-dependent effects that, in the examined heads, match the phases their gates prefer. supplementary gate-cycling intervention on five models with non-overlapping windows complements this association (Appendix H). Retrieval diagnostics and position bias. Zoologys multi-query associative recall isolates major capability gap between attention and efficient sequence models [3]. The copying results of Jelassi et al. [17] and induction-circuit studies [4, 24] motivate our synthetic retrieval task. Lost in the Middle establishes broad U-shaped sensitivity to absolute target position [19], and RULER shows that easy needle tests can overstate usable context length [16]. The Pitfalls of KV Cache Compression further shows that aggregate scores hide instructionand method-specific failures [5]. We therefore match the mean and variance of the targets absolute position across residue groups and report retrieval by phase rather than only mean accuracy. Optimization and specialization. Max-margin analyses show that gradient descent can turn softmax attention into hard token selectors [32, 33], although entropy concentration can also be pathological [43]. Chen et al. [6] prove staged multi-head task allocation in in-context linear regression, and Yang et al. [40] analyze population gradient flow in symmetric two-headed classification transformer. Most closely related, Yüksel et al. [42] analyze near-symmetric heads that first compete for dominant sparse pattern and later specialize through competition and cooperation. High-dimensional SGD likewise exhibits sequential head specialization [30], while generic softmax factorization can bias gradient flow toward low-entropy outputs [34]. We therefore do not claim the first theory of attention hardening, symmetry breaking, or division of labor. Our theory (Section 5) concerns an idealized induction model of retrieval from compressed memory. In this model, optimal compressors select sharply, gradient flow from small initialization reaches, with high probability, selection that persists across inputs, and nothing guarantees that heads choose distinct positions.
